seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

msIdentifier.repository: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: Dear Pound: Thanks for your card and good opinion of the Hades episode. I sent you some days ago express the Eolus episode. I am very sorry I did not receive your new article about the novel (?). Perhaps Mr Edward Marsh of the Home Office could help you to send these things quickly. I have not seen any number of The Little Review since the June issue. My American publisher sent me several long controversial articles about Ulysses which appeared in papers there – one very benevolent , by Mr Hecht. As he is a collaborator may I beg you to convey my thanks to him when you have occasion to write to him. I shall send you as quickly as I can the Lestrygonians and after that the Hamlet chapter (Scylla and Charybdis). I received your M.O. (£10) and thank you very much. If you need a collective receipt for the £30 I shall send it on demand. I regret that Mr Davray has not kept his promise in the Mercure de France. Mr Brock wrote an article , I believe, in the Times (lit. supplement) about Exiles and suggests that the Pioneers or the Stage Society do it. I shall write several postcards accordingly.

I shall be glad to hear how and what you yourself are doing. For my part I am house-hunting – a difficult business as furnished flats are very rare and dear. I was quite comfortable in these rooms till the adjoining hospital bought the house. Miss Weaver tells me that a criticism of my book appeared in a Japanese review. I should like to see it as a curiosity. I can get it translated here by a Japanese whom I know, Mr Oikawa. There is a proposal also to translate it into Danish. Meanwhile in 6 months 40 copies have been sold – which is very encouraging. I hope your good wishes about my wretched eyes will come true – 4 attacks in 16 months! I shall send you a letter for Mr Lewis when I write again. One of his pictures was hung here in a show – a Russian madonna . He sent me a copy of Tarr
. My publisher has not yet sent copies of Exiles here! This explains why I did not send you a presentation copy. He has not sent copies to the critics whose names I gave him (Swiss, Italian, French). I shall write to him also several postcards.

My son Giorgio is fast developing into the swimming champion of Switzerland. He swam 6 kilometres yesterday and the day before 2 km., fully dressed and with weighted boots. His performances are watched by an admiring population – but he would need an extra bread allowance. We have white bread here, thank God, but the coal for the winter is a problem. I have a very nice doctor. He says: Eat all you can, don’t get up early in the morning and amuse yourself.

closer.salute: With kind regards to Mrs Pound and yourself in which my wife joins

div.note: JJ sent a copy of “Hades,” the sixth episode of Ulysses, to Pound in July 1918, along with a copy for Harriet Shaw Weaver and her magazine The Egoist (LI 115). It recounts Leopold Bloom’s journey by carriage with other Dublin men to Glasnevin cemetery in Dublin, where there is a chapel funeral service for an acquaintance, Paddy Dignam. The episode loosely parallels Odysseus’s visit to the underworld in Book 11 of The Odyssey, where he meets many ghosts and seeks out the prophet Tiresias for help in returning to his island home, Ithaca. “Hades” appeared in The Little Review, vol. 5, no. 5 (September 1918): 15-37.

The seventh episode of Ulysses, “Aeolus,” is set in the Dublin offices of the Freeman’s Journal, where Leopold Bloom and Stephen Dedalus are on the premises but do not meet. Stephen joins in with a group of men who are entertaining each other by reciting windy speeches and trading witty banter, and tells a story about two aging Dublin women as he leads the group off for drinks at a pub. The Homeric parallel is found in Book 10 of The Odyssey, where Odysseus meets Aeolus, guardian of the winds and king of the island of Aeolia. Aeolus gifts Odysseus with a bag in which stormy winds are confined, but his curious sailors open it and release a storm that blows all ships back to Aeolia. “Aeolus” appeared in The Little Review, vol. 5, no. 6 (October 1918): 26-51.

Probably Pound’s article, “Books Current,” Future, vol. 2, no. 6 (May 1918): 161-63, in which he reviewed the recent Egoist Ltd. edition of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (March 1918). A Portrait, wrote Pound, “has become almost the prose bible of a few people,” and contains “clear-cut and definite sentences” and a “swift alternation of subjective beauty and external shabbiness, squalor, and sordidness” (161-62). Pound also took the opportunity to comment on a new edition of Chamber Music issued by Elkin Mathews in London (January 1918), praising the poems’ “clean-cut ivory finish, and … the interest of the rhythms, the cross run of the beat and the word, as of a stiff wind cutting the ripple-tops of bright water” (162).

Edward Marsh (1872-1953), translator and editor, had assisted JJ with obtaining a grant of £100 from the British Civil List while serving as assistant private secretary to British Prime Minister H.H. Asquith (see JJ to Pound, 14 September 1916, notes). With the fall of Asquith’s government in December 1916, Marsh acted as private secretary to Winston Churchill, by then Minister of Munitions, and served in that capacity for several more years.

“Calypso,” the fourth episode of Ulysses, appeared in the New York magazine, The Little Review, vol. 5, no. 2 (June 1918): 39-52. The issue, “An American Number,” also contained work by Wallace Stevens, William Carlos Williams, Amy Lowell, Carl Sandburg, Djuna Barnes, and others. The section called “The Reader Critic” printed letters to the editor attacking JJ for incomprehensibility (“I swear I’ve read his ‘Ulysses’ and haven’t found out yet what it’s about, who is who or where” [54]) and immorality (“Justify some of Joyce’s obscene commonplaces taken from life neither for power nor beauty nor for any reason but to arrest attention, cheap Bowery vileness” [56]), followed by defenses of JJ’s method and art by “jh,” the magazine’s coeditor, Jane Heap (1883-1964).

By August 1918, the New York publisher B.W. Huebsch (1876-1964) had published the first edition of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, the first American editions of Dubliners and Exiles, and would shortly issue the first authorized American edition of Chamber Music in September 1918.

Ben Hecht (1894-1964), journalist, playwright, and novelist, was born in New York, raised in Wisconsin, and became a member of a group of writers in Chicago just after World War I. JJ possibly refers here to his piece, “Boob Babble,” Chicago Daily News (3 July 1918): 6, which praised JJ as “a capable and persuasive writer…. Reading Joyce and understanding him is no more difficult than listening to a crowd of people talking and understanding them, their natures and their motives. The thing requires a degree of intelligence and sophistication. And until reading becomes for the muzhik as well as the local Brahmin and the curious faithful something more than a perfunctory stare at printed words, the hee-haw chorus will continue to greet Joyce and his followers, good and bad.” For the chaotic, often combative reactions to the serialized Ulysses, both favorable and unfavorable, in Chicago newspapers in 1918, see Robert Billings and Donald Zochert, “Ulysses and the Hog Butchers,” James Joyce Quarterly, vol. 11, no. 1 (Fall 1973): 27-32.

Hecht’s work appeared in The Little Review beginning in 1915, and included book reviews, critical essays, and impressionistic prose pieces. For example, the May 1918 number featured his “Nocturne,” the story of a person wandering the city streets at night and entering a movie theater where he alternately watches the film and members of the audience (45-52). The June 1918 number contained his short piece “Lust,” an account of a woman who plays violin at an inn and, finding the city dirty and repulsive, commits suicide during a vacation in the country (14-20). Pound wrote of him: “Hecht is an asset. Hard reading and a bit heavy, but [h]e is the sound stuff, that with right pages open to him can develop” (Pound/The Little Review : The Letters of Ezra Pound to Margaret Anderson: The Little Review Correspondence, ed. Thomas L. Scott and Melvin J. Friedman [New York: New Directions, 1988], 220).

“Lestrygonians,” the eighth episode of Ulysses, appeared in two numbers of The Little Review, vol. 5, nos. 9-10/11 (January and February-March 1919): 27-50, 58-62. The episode follows Leopold Bloom through Dublin as he encounters an old flame, Josie Breen, has lunch in a pub, and afterwards spots Blazes Boylan, the young man he knows will have a rendezvous with his wife Molly later that day, and avoids him by escaping through the gate of the National Museum. The Homeric parallel is found in Book 10 of The Odyssey, where many of Odysseus’s men are devoured by giant cannibals, the Lestrygonians, and only Odysseus and his crew escape the deadly island.

“Scylla and Charybdis,” the ninth episode of Ulysses, appeared in two numbers of The Little Review, vol. 5, no. 12-vol. 6, no. 1 (April and May 1919): 30-43, 17-35. In this episode, Stephen Dedalus presents his theory about Shakespeare and Hamlet to a group of writers and librarians in the National Library; as Stephen and Buck Mulligan leave the building, Leopold Bloom politely passes between them. In Book 12 of The Odyssey, Odysseus sails his ship perilously between the monster Scylla and the deadly whirlpool Charybdis, losing several crew to Scylla.

Payments for the printing of Ulysses in The Little Review. In a letter to Nora Barnacle dated 10 September 1917, Pound mentioned that he hoped to pay JJ £50 or more, in due course, for the serialization (Pound/Joyce 125-26).

Henry D. Davray (1873-1944), a French critic who contributed regularly on English literature to the Mercure de France, discussed JJ’s Exiles and other writings in “Lettres anglaises,” published in the Mercure, vol. 121, no. 495 (1 February 1919): 512-18. See JJ to Pound, 24 July 1917, notes.

Arthur Clutton-Brock (1868–1924), English essayist, critic, and journalist. In “The Mind to Suffer,” Times Literary Supplement (25 July 1918): 346, he wrote that Exiles “reveals resources of spiritual passion and constructive power which should greatly cheer the friends of [JJ’s] talent.” After a lengthy discussion of the play’s plot and themes, Clutton-Brock asked: “Will not the Stage Society or the Pioneers let us and the author see this play, so that its shortcomings may become apparent to him and its virtues be brought home to us with their full force?”
Despite the efforts of JJ and others, the London-based Incorporated Stage Society did not produce Exiles at this time (see JJ to Pound, 5 June 1917, notes). The Society finally presented the play at London’s Regent Theatre on 14 and 15 February 1926, with W.G. Fay as director. The Pioneer Players, a London theater society known for producing banned and controversial plays, never staged Exiles (see JJ to Pound, 30 March 1917, notes).
JJ and family moved from Universitätstrasse 38 to Universitätstrasse 29 in late October 1918.

Maja Maag, in Hellerup, Denmark, had written JJ circa July 1918 that she was considering translating A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man into Danish (LI 116). A Portrait was translated into Danish by Ove Brusendorff and published as Portræt af kunstneren som ungt menneske (Copenhagen: Athenaeum Dansk Forlag, 1941).

JJ wrote Harriet Shaw Weaver on 29 July 1918: “After nine weeks’ illness I am at last able to read and write again” (LI 115). Despite eye surgery in August 1917, JJ was still suffering from painful attacks.

The English painter and writer Wyndham Lewis (1882-1957) created “Russian Madonna” or “Russian Scene” (pen and ink, chalk, and watercolor) in 1912; it depicts a mother and child in the manner of a Russian icon. The painting was part of an exhibition, Englische Moderne Malerei, organized by the Contemporary Arts Society in London, and hung at the Zurich Kunsthaus from 8 to 28 August 1918. Together with Lewis’s one painting, the show featured a total of 107 paintings by twenty-five artists, including Vanessa Bell, Max Beerbohm, Frederick Etchells, Roger Fry, Duncan Grant, Augustus John, Paul Nash, Will Rothenstein, Walter Sickert, and others. Instrumental in organizing the Zurich exhibition was a British artist, Horace Taylor (1881-1934), who had two paintings in the show and wrote a three-page introduction, in German, for the exhibition catalogue (“Englische moderne Malerei,” Ausstellung 8. - 28. August 1918 [Zurich: Kunsthaus Zürich, 1918]: 3-5). It was through Taylor that JJ met the English painter Frank Budgen (1882-1971), who, like Taylor, was working at the time for the British government at the Ministry of Information in Zurich. Budgen tells of meeting JJ at Taylor’s pension “in the early summer of 1918” (Frank Budgen, James Joyce and the Making of Ulysses [1934; rpt. Bloomington: Indiana University Press, 1960], 9-15; see also Ellmann, JJ 429). Lewis’s “Russian Madonna” was acquired by London’s Victoria and Albert Museum in 1919. He later produced several noted portrait drawings of JJ, whom he met for the first time in the summer of 1920. His portrait drawings and paintings of Pound are also celebrated.

Tarr, a novel by Wyndham Lewis, was serialized in the London magazine Egoist in 1916-1917 and published as a book in 1918 by the Egoist Ltd. in London and by Alfred A. Knopf in New York – in each case with significant variants. The story is laid in “bourgeois-bohemian” Paris before World War I, and follows two artists, the Englishman Frederick Tarr and the German Otto Kreisler, as they contend with and for aesthetics, women, and social philosophies. JJ asked his friend, the English painter and writer Frank Budgen (1882-1971), to read Tarr for him, as JJ had “still to read it myself and write to [Lewis] about it” (LII 419). JJ tried to get the novel reviewed in the Neue Zürcher Zeitung and the Zürcher Post (LI 122), but by late February 1919 neither had yet done so (LII 437).

B.W. Huebsch in New York published Exiles in May 1918 simultaneously with its publication in London by Grant Richards. At various points, JJ expressed urgency or frustration about copies reaching him or persons he had designated to receive it (LII 418, 420).
Giorgio Joyce (1905-1976) became a professional singer, making his début in 1929. He married Helen Kastor Fleischman in 1930, and in February 1932 their son, Stephen James Joyce, was born.
